video_title: Inside the Fastest-Growing Category in AI: Scott Wu, CEO of $26B Cognition
gist: Scott Wu, CEO of Cognition (maker of Devin), details how the company reached ~$500M revenue in under three years on $2.5B raised at a $26B valuation, why it acquired Windsurf over a single weekend, and why it is betting on staying model-neutral and independent rather than becoming or selling to a frontier lab. He argues tokens are a dead productivity metric, that benchmarks are becoming trivially solvable while long-horizon and ill-defined tasks remain the real frontier, and that the next unlock is capacity (single-use, self-driving software) rather than efficiency.

themes.theme: Cognition's growth math and unit economics

insights.claim: Cognition reached roughly $500M in revenue in under three years, having raised over $2.5B to date at a last valuation of $26B.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete revenue-to-valuation anchor (~52x) for pricing private AI coding-agent comparables and any secondary exposure.

insights.claim: Cognition's named enterprise logos include Goldman Sachs, Mercedes-Benz, Citi, Dell, Santander, NASA, the US Navy, and the US Army, showing autonomous coding agents have already cleared procurement at regulated financial institutions and defense agencies.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Bank and defense adoption signals the compliance barrier to agentic coding is already breached, pulling forward the addressable market for incumbents' internal dev-tool budgets.

insights.claim: Cognition uses Devin to build Devin, with roughly 95% of its own code now written by the agent — a live proof point that agentic coding can carry near-total authorship inside a frontier product company.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: The vendor's own 95% internal substitution rate is the most aggressive public datapoint for how far engineering headcount leverage can be pushed.
insights.quote: Like 95% of the code or something is written by Devon.

insights.claim: Cognition's total code shipped — PRs and lines — roughly 7x'd in the six months before this interview, meaning most of the compounding in agentic coding output happened very recently rather than over the three-to-four-year life of the category.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Suggests the inflection in agent usefulness is a 2026 phenomenon; adoption models built on 2024-25 curves understate the slope.

insights.claim: Cognition's customers grew their Devin usage roughly 11-12x over the prior six months, indicating expansion inside existing accounts — not just new logos — is driving the revenue ramp.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Net-revenue-retention-style expansion above 10x is the metric to watch for whether coding-agent revenue is durable or land-and-churn.
insights.quote: our customers in the last six months or so have also grown their usage in something in the range of like 11 to 12x

insights.claim: Wu frames 3x year-over-year growth as underperformance in the coding-agent category, implying the underlying adoption rate is faster than that and that vendors growing merely 3x are losing share.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Gives a hurdle rate: any AI coding vendor pitching 3x growth should be read as a share loser, not a winner.
insights.quote: if we frankly if we only 3xed year-over-year or whatever it is, you know, we'd be we'd be lagging the market

insights.claim: Wu argues token consumption is now a discredited productivity metric and declares the 'token max era' ran only from January to May of 2026, with buyers shifting to outcome- and KPI-based measurement of AI value.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: If enterprises stop paying for tokens and start paying for outcomes, per-token inference revenue at the labs decouples from the value captured at the application layer.
insights.quote: I kind I say the token max era, you know, lasted from January to to May of 2026, roughly.

themes.theme: Windsurf acquisition mechanics and post-merger playbook

insights.claim: Cognition negotiated and closed the entire Windsurf acquisition over a single weekend — first contact Friday evening after the Google aqui-hire news broke, announcement ready Monday morning.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Shows distressed AI assets can transact in 48 hours; buyers with pre-formed conviction win these, so watch who is positioned when the next lab aqui-hire strands a go-to-market org.

insights.claim: At the time of the Windsurf acquisition Cognition was only 35-40 people with roughly $70-80M of revenue run rate, while Windsurf had around 200 people — meaning the acquirer absorbed a company five times its headcount.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Anchors the revenue trajectory: from ~$75M run rate at the deal to ~$500M within about eleven months, a 6-7x in under a year.
insights.quote: we were doing um in the range of 70 or 80 million of revenue run rate at the time

insights.claim: The strategic logic of buying Windsurf was that the IDE (where a developer reads code) and the asynchronous remote agent (which the developer delegates to) need shared codebase knowledge and session handoff, so owning both sides is a product requirement rather than a bolt-on.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Predicts consolidation pressure on pure-play IDEs and pure-play async agents alike; standalone players on either side are structurally disadvantaged.

insights.claim: Cognition deliberately refused to force a 30- or 60-day product merge, instead shipping both Windsurf and Devin independently and letting real usage and new features pull the products together over roughly a year into paired Devin Cloud and Devin Desktop.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: A reusable post-merger integration model for fast-moving software M&A: preserve both revenue streams and let feature gravity, not a deadline, drive convergence.
insights.quote: letting the actual usage and the the new features that we're building the kind of next paradigms that we were getting to like letting those like pull the products together more gradually rather than forcing it

insights.claim: The host cites a $60B Cursor/SpaceX deal as the current M&A backdrop in AI coding, with Cognition positioned as the notable holdout choosing to remain independent.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Consolidation of coding-agent assets into much larger strategic acquirers sets the comparable valuation ceiling and raises the odds Cognition is itself an eventual target or IPO candidate.

themes.theme: Independence, model neutrality, and the application-layer moat

insights.claim: Wu explicitly rejects the prevailing narrative that winning in AI coding requires either being a frontier lab or selling to one, and positions Cognition's complete model neutrality across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google as a competitive asset.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: If model-neutral application layers can hold enterprise relationships, model commoditization accrues value to the app layer rather than to any single lab.
insights.quote: there's been a narrative out there that oh like in order to win you have to be a lab yourself or you have to go sell to a lab

insights.claim: Wu's differentiation thesis is that durable value sits in the 'value layer' — reorganizing how teams plan, write specs, do design and user research in the AI era — rather than in the raw intelligence layer, because organizational change cannot be delivered by throwing a chatbot over the wall.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Implies the defensible margin in AI deployment is services-adjacent change management, which favors vendors with deployed-engineering motions over pure API sellers.

insights.claim: Wu rejects the recursive-superintelligence-singleton scenario in which one or two entities own everything after AGI, and frames independent tooling as necessary so people can control their own intelligence.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: A market-structure call: the winner-take-all AGI thesis that underpins some lab valuations is being contested by a major application-layer operator.
insights.quote: you just take over the entire world and then there's just like one entity that rules the world

themes.theme: Government as an underserved software market and AI policy

insights.claim: Wu identifies government and DC as possibly the single largest concentration of demand for software that cannot be built for lack of engineers, with archaic systems and broken processes as the addressable target — the reason Cognition spent Independence Day in DC.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: GovTech modernization becomes economically feasible when agents supply the labor; watch federal software budgets and incumbent government-systems integrators for displacement risk.
insights.quote: imagine going to the DMV and and it actually worked

insights.claim: Wu draws an explicit analogy between AI policy today and early-internet debates over whether a handful of corporations would control the network, arguing the open-internet outcome should be deliberately replicated for AI before all businesses are built on it.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Signals that application-layer incumbents will lobby for openness and against lab concentration — a policy tailwind for model-neutral vendors and a regulatory risk for vertically integrated labs.

insights.claim: Wu dismisses the 'six months to singularity' view, arguing that many real-world bottlenecks are not intelligence-soluble — organizational change, processes that take time, and hard limits on available GPU compute.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: A capability optimist who is a timeline skeptic; supports positioning for a multi-year deployment grind rather than a discontinuous takeoff trade.

insights.claim: Wu argues essentially any benchmark is now solvable because defining a benchmark means you have already specified the task, the success criteria, and example behavior — at which point RL reliably teaches the model to do it.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Benchmark scores are losing information value as a model-differentiation signal; discount eval-based marketing and look for performance on unspecified, open-ended work.
insights.quote: we're kind of getting to the point where you can solve basically any benchmark

insights.claim: Wu locates the real capability frontier in amorphous, long-time-horizon tasks with no clean success definition — his example being a ten-year strategic decision whose feedback signal only arrives a decade later, versus a program you can simply run and check.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Predicts which white-collar work automates first (verifiable, short-loop) versus last (judgment, long-loop) — a direct map for labor-displacement exposure by role.
insights.quote: if you're asking it to make a 10-year strategic decision, well, it's kind of hard to get the data on whether you did that right or wrong until you've waited 10 years out

insights.claim: Wu states that in pure knowledge work there is nothing humans do that AI cannot do, because human brains are computers and neural networks were modeled on them — expressing no long-run ceiling on capability while still rejecting near-term takeoff.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Separates the capability question from the timing question, the distinction that matters for sizing knowledge-work automation exposure over a decade rather than a quarter.
insights.quote: there is nothing that humans do that AI can't do

themes.theme: What a coding agent actually is — the Devin origin

insights.claim: Devin's first real task, in December 2023, was fixing a failed local MongoDB setup for co-founder Walden after Stack Overflow answers failed — the moment the team first believed autonomous coding agents were possible.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Dates the category's founding insight to late 2023, framing today's ~$500M revenue as a roughly two-and-a-half-year commercialization cycle.

insights.claim: Wu defines a coding agent as exactly two capabilities combined: encyclopedic knowledge of every possible error and its causes, plus the ability to actually run commands and diagnose live system state — the pairing that made the MongoDB fix work where search alone failed.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: A crisp test for evaluating agent products: knowledge-only tools (completion, chat) are structurally weaker than those with execution and inspection rights.

themes.theme: The abundance thesis: capacity over efficiency

insights.claim: Wu argues the real economic unlock from AI coding is capacity — how much more software can exist — not efficiency, and that focusing on doing existing work in a third of the time measures the smaller half of the opportunity.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-coding trade from a cost-cutting story (fewer engineers) to a volume story (far more software built), which implies rising rather than falling total software spend.
insights.quote: the real unlock is not in efficiency but in um capacity

insights.claim: Wu predicts single-use software and self-driving software will exist — software generated on the fly for one purpose — extending 'software is eating the world' to domains where hand-writing every line was previously the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: Disposable, generated software threatens the seat-based SaaS model for long-tail workflow tools while expanding demand for compute and data infrastructure underneath it.
insights.quote: single use software is going to exist like self-driving software is going to exist

insights.claim: During Cognition's seed round Wu proposed settling the remaining valuation gap with a heads-up poker match whose winner would dictate terms — a spread he says was worth about 1% of the company in retrospect — and Peter Thiel shut the idea down before the deal was negotiated conventionally.
insights.speaker: Scott Wu
insights.so_what: A 1% seed-round term spread at a company now valued at $26B would be worth roughly $260M today — a vivid illustration of how small early-round concessions compound.
insights.quote: It would have been for in retrospect, it would have been for like 1% of the company or something
